knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,

Latent transition analysis (LTA) models change in latent states over
repeated occasions (Collins & Lanza, 2010). At every occasion, each unit
belongs to one of a small number of unobserved states, defined, as in latent
class or profile analysis, by their distributions on the observed indicators.
Change is the movement of units between these states from one occasion to the
next. LTA estimates the states, how units are distributed over them at the
start, and how likely each move is.

## What latent transition analysis is

**States are latent.** The indicators measure the state of a unit at an
occasion with error. Classifying each occasion separately, for instance with
one latent profile analysis per occasion, and cross-tabulating the
assignments treats every misclassification as a change of state and
overstates instability. LTA estimates the states and the transitions in one
model, so the transition probabilities are free of classification error
(Collins & Lanza, 2010).

**The model has three parts.** With $S_{jt}$ the state of unit $j$ at
occasion $t$ and $Y_{jt}$ its indicators,

- the measurement model $P(Y_{jt} \mid S_{jt} = k)$ defines each state: means
  and variances for continuous indicators, response probabilities for
  categorical ones;
- the initial probabilities $\delta_k = P(S_{j1} = k)$ give the distribution
  of the states at the first occasion;
- the transition probabilities $\tau_{kl} = P(S_{jt} = l \mid S_{j,t-1} = k)$
  give the probability of moving from state $k$ to state $l$; each row of the
  transition matrix sums to one, the diagonal holds the probabilities of
  staying, and the off-diagonal cells the direction of change.

**Default assumptions make the transitions interpretable.** The measurement
model is the same at every occasion (measurement invariance), so a state
means the same thing throughout and a transition is a change of state rather
than a change of the states' definitions. The next state depends only on the
current one (the first-order Markov property), and the transition
probabilities are the same at every move (homogeneity). Each of these can be
relaxed, as the last section shows.

**LTA is a hidden Markov model.** The states form a Markov chain that is not
observed directly; only the indicators are. In the terminology of hidden
Markov models (Rabiner, 1989), the measurement model gives the emission
distributions. `lta()` estimates the model by maximum likelihood with the
EM algorithm, computing the posterior probabilities of the states with the
forward-backward recursions.

**Group classes add heterogeneity in change.** A single transition matrix
assumes that all units change in the same way. With latent group classes,
each class has its own initial and transition probabilities over the same
states, a mixed Markov model (van de Pol & Langeheine, 1990). The classes are
types of dynamics: for example, units that leave an unfavourable state
quickly and units that remain in it. The mover-stayer model (Goodman, 1961)
is the special case with one class of units that never change state.

**The output describes change:** the prevalence of each state over time, the
stability of each state (the diagonal of the transition matrix), the most
likely moves out of each state, the differences in dynamics between group
classes and, with covariates, the predictors of the initial state and of
each transition.

## Data

`course_engagement` is simulated and has one row per course enrolment: 1,422
enrolments from 106 students. The simulation is calibrated to the engagement
data of students followed through a full study programme (Saqr & López-Pernas,
2021; Saqr et al., 2023): its scales, spread, correlations and the persistence
of engagement across courses follow those data, while no value of the source
is retained. `lta()` needs three kinds of variables.

- **Group:** `student` identifies whose occasions belong together.
- **Occasion order:** `sequence` is the position of each course in the
  student's history. Students can have different numbers of occasions (10 to
  15 here).
- **Indicators:** five activity measures (`browse`, `lectures`, `forum_read`,
  `forum_post`, `attendance`), each standardized within course, so 0 is the
  course average.

The data were generated from two engagement profiles and two kinds of
students, committed and wavering, whose stationary probabilities of an
engaged enrolment are about 0.8 and 0.25; engagement changes along each
student's sequence (`?course_engagement`). `attendance` is generated from the
four click measures, so the indicators are correlated within profiles.

```{r setup}
library(latents)
vars <- c("browse", "lectures", "forum_read", "forum_post", "attendance")
```

## Numbers of profiles and group classes

`enumerate_classes()` with `time` compares transition models. Because
attendance depends on the other indicators, the candidates estimate full
within-profile covariances (`covariance_model = "full"`); with a diagonal
structure, an additional profile absorbs that dependence (see the
[multilevel latent profile analysis](https://pak.dynasite.org/latents/articles/lpa.html)
vignette).

```{r enumerate, warning = FALSE}
grid <- enumerate_classes(course_engagement, vars = vars, id = "student",
                          time = "sequence", covariance_model = "full",
                          n_profiles = 2:3, n_group_classes = 1:3,
                          n_starts = 5, seed = 1)
grid
get_best(grid)
```

The BIC (Schwarz, 1978) selects two profiles and two group classes. That
candidate has no estimate on a boundary and reaches its best log likelihood
from every start; all candidates with three profiles have boundary estimates
and reach their best solutions from a single start. A multilevel latent
profile analysis of the same data favours additional group classes, which
absorb the serial dependence that it does not model; LTA models that
dependence and selects the generating structure.

## Fit

The `lta()` function requires indicators (`vars`), a group identifier
(`id`), and occasion order (`time`). The arguments `n_profiles` and
`n_group_classes` specify the latent structure; `n_starts` and `seed`
control repeated estimation from reproducible starting values.

```{r fit}
moves <- lta(course_engagement, vars = vars, id = "student",
             time = "sequence", covariance_model = "full",
             n_profiles = 2, n_group_classes = 2, n_starts = 10, seed = 1)
moves
```

Profile 1 (58.9% of the enrolments) lies 0.42 to 0.64 standard deviations
above the course mean on all indicators and profile 2 (41.1%) 0.61 to 0.91
below it: engaged and disengaged enrolments.

The `"starts"` table reports the log likelihood reached by each start.
Replication of the selected likelihood supports numerical stability but
does not establish that the global maximum has been found.

```{r starts}
get_results(moves, "starts")
```

All ten starts reach the log likelihood of -8188.

## Profiles

The profile plot displays estimated indicator means and the estimated share
of occasions in each profile. For a transition model, `plot()` without an
explicit view instead displays transition matrices.

```{r profiles}
plot_profiles(moves)
```

The profile heatmap expresses each mean in standard deviations from the
indicator's overall mean, facilitating comparison across indicators.

```{r heatmap}
plot_profiles(moves, what = "heatmap")
```

## Starting probabilities

The `"initial"` table reports initial profile probabilities (`probability`),
profile prevalence across occasions (`prevalence`), and estimated group-class
proportions (`group_class_probability`).

```{r initial}
get_results(moves, "initial")
```

Group class 2 (63% of the students) starts engaged with probability 0.833 and
is engaged at 78.9% of its occasions; group class 1 (37%) starts engaged with
probability 0.271 and is engaged at 24.6% of its occasions. These prevalences
match the stationary probabilities of the committed and wavering students in
the simulation, about 0.8 and 0.25.

## Transitions

The `"transitions"` table reports the probability of moving from state
`from` to state `to` at the next occasion. Probabilities sum to one within
each origin state and group class. The column `stable` identifies transitions
that retain the same state; `expected_count` reports the posterior expected
transition count. A row with `estimated = FALSE` lacks information for
estimating that transition distribution.

```{r transitions}
get_results(moves, "transitions")
```

The group classes differ mainly in recovery from disengagement. A committed
student (group class 2) who is disengaged in one course is engaged in the
next with probability 0.408; a wavering student (group class 1) with
probability 0.068, remaining disengaged with probability 0.932. Engagement is
stable in both classes (0.884 and 0.774). Every transition rests on enough
expected moves to be estimated (`supported` and `estimated` are `TRUE`).

The transition plot displays one matrix per group class, with current
profiles in rows and next-occasion profiles in columns.

```{r transition-plot}
plot_transitions(moves)
```

## Sequences

The sequence plot displays one row per group, coloured by the most probable
profile at each occasion, as the sequence index plots of sequence analysis do
(Saqr et al., 2024). These modal assignments summarize the fitted
sequences but omit classification uncertainty.

```{r sequences, fig.height = 6}
plot_sequences(moves)
```

## Classification

The `"entropy"` table reports relative entropy for occasions and groups
(Ramaswamy et al., 1993). With more than one class, a value of 1 indicates
certain posterior membership; 0 indicates equal posterior probabilities
across classes for every case. Entropy summarizes classification separation
under the fitted model.

```{r entropy}
get_results(moves, "entropy")
```

Occasions are classified clearly (0.943), students much less so (0.654).
Under the transition model a student's class rests on the dynamics of a
sequence of 10 to 15 states, and a wavering student who happens to stay
engaged for several courses resembles a committed one. The cross-tabulation
with the generating labels shows the consequence.

```{r recovery}
get_results(moves, "assignments", data = course_engagement,
            truth = c("engagement", "student_type"))
```

The profiles recover 825 of the 837 engaged and 575 of the 585 disengaged
enrolments (98.6% and 98.3%). Group class 2 contains 61 of the 62 committed
students and 9 of the 44 wavering ones. Diagnostic plots display per-case
uncertainty within each profile (`what = "entropy"`) and posterior
probabilities of assigned profiles (`what = "posteriors"`).

```{r entropy-plot}
plot_diagnostics(moves, what = "entropy")
```

```{r posteriors-plot}
plot_diagnostics(moves, what = "posteriors")
```

## Transition networks

The estimated transitions can be represented as networks. `get_tna()`
returns a network pooled across group classes; `get_group_tna()` returns one
network per class. Both functions produce
[tna](https://cran.r-project.org/package=tna) objects (Tikka et al., 2025)
that can be displayed with `plot()` and analysed further with tna or with
[Nestimate](https://cran.r-project.org/package=Nestimate) (Saqr et al.,
2026), which accepts `tna` and `group_tna` objects.

```{r networks, message = FALSE, eval = requireNamespace("tna", quietly = TRUE)}
plot(get_tna(moves))
plot(get_group_tna(moves))
```

## Beyond homogeneous transitions

Several extensions permit alternative specifications of temporal dependence
and measurement:

- `transition_covariates` lets covariates shift the transition
  probabilities: the log odds of moving to each other profile rather than
  staying. A covariate may change over occasions.
- `initial_covariates` lets covariates shift the starting profile.
- `transitions = "occasion"` estimates a separate transition matrix for each
  move.
- `measurement = "occasion"` lets the profiles' means and variances differ by
  occasion.
- `order = 2` makes the next profile depend on the two previous ones.
- `mover_stayer = TRUE` adds a class of groups that never change profile
  (Goodman, 1961).

`enumerate_classes(..., time = "sequence")` compares numbers of profiles and
group classes, and `bootstrap_lrt()` tests a model against a nested one.

The following example examines whether `previous_grade`, which varies
across courses, is associated with transition probabilities:

```{r grade}
grade <- lta(course_engagement, vars = vars, id = "student",
             time = "sequence", covariance_model = "full", n_profiles = 2,
             n_group_classes = 2, transition_covariates = "previous_grade",
             n_starts = 10, seed = 1)
get_results(grade, "transition_coefficients")
```

The odds ratios of `previous_grade` are between 0.71 and 1.30, and every 95%
interval of its log-odds coefficients includes zero. These results provide limited
evidence of an association between previous grade and transitions in this
example; they do not establish the absence of an association. A second-order
model, in which the next profile depends on the two previous states, and a
mover-stayer model can also be compared with the first-order specification
using BIC:

```{r second-order, warning = FALSE}
second <- lta(course_engagement, vars = vars, id = "student",
              time = "sequence", covariance_model = "full", n_profiles = 2,
              n_group_classes = 2, order = 2, n_starts = 10, seed = 1)
stayer <- lta(course_engagement, vars = vars, id = "student",
              time = "sequence", covariance_model = "full", n_profiles = 2,
              mover_stayer = TRUE, n_starts = 10, seed = 1)
BIC(moves, grade, second, stayer)
```

```{r check-extensions, include = FALSE}
slopes <- subset(get_results(grade, "transition_coefficients"),
                 term == "previous_grade")
stopifnot(all(slopes$conf_low < 0 & slopes$conf_high > 0),
          BIC(moves) < BIC(grade), BIC(moves) < BIC(second),
          BIC(moves) < BIC(stayer))
```

For these data, BIC is lower for the first-order model with two group
classes than for any extension: the grade covariate (BIC higher by 15), the
second-order dependence (by 32) and the mover-stayer structure (by 10).
Extended models provide transition and initial-state logit coefficients,
with Wald standard errors when supported by the fitted model, and
occasion-specific probability summaries.

## Assumptions

- By default the next profile depends only on the current profile and the
  group class, and transition probabilities are the same at every occasion;
  the arguments above relax each of these.
- Profiles have the same definition at every occasion unless
  `measurement = "occasion"`.
- Indicators are independent within a profile under the default diagonal
  covariance; `covariance_model = "full"` or a non-diagonal `model` relaxes
  it, as here.
